processing: The aerial parts of the vine are dried and cut. There is no oxidation or roasting.
harvest_season: No prized harvest is recorded; as with other leafy herbs, it is gathered during the growing season and dried.
appearance_dry: Cut, muted green leaf and stem fragments with some bits of flower.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale yellow-green to light gold.
appearance_wet: Soft olive-green leaf and stem pieces.
taste_profile: Mild and grassy with an earthy undertone, a quiet cup without much sweetness or bite.

brewing.notes: About a tablespoon of dried herb per cup of boiling water. Steep times vary widely; ten minutes is a sensible start, and a stronger cup can use double the herb.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage or season, in bags or as cut dried herb, and often blended into bedtime mixes. Look for the name Passiflora incarnata, sometimes sold as maypop; other species in the genus are less studied. As with other dried herbs, it is best used while the colour and smell are still fresh.
description:
Passionflower tea is made from the dried leaves, stems and flowers of Passiflora incarnata, a climbing vine native to the southeastern United States. It is the same family as passion fruit, but this cup tastes nothing like fruit.

Processing goes no further than drying and cutting, as is typical of leafy herbal teas. So what you get is the plain flavour of the plant.

Expect a mild, grassy cup with some earthiness. It pours out rather shy, so a generous amount of herb and a long, covered steep serve it best.

It is drunk mostly as an evening tea, for its traditional use against anxiety and poor sleep. Research is limited: in one trial of an extract for insomnia, results were no better than placebo overall, so take sleep promises with caution.
history: Records are patchy. Native Americans are reported to have used the root in poultices, and Indigenous healers are said to have used the plant as a sedative. A monograph credits the Spanish physician Nicolás Monardes with first documenting it in 1569. Little is documented about the tea as a commercial product.
